To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of pollutant exposure and climate warming on polar bears are likely to interact and that the effects of pollutants on polar bears may add significantly to the effects of the loss of their sea-ice habitat.

(i) climate warming will result in increased fasting periods and thus increases in tissue concentrations of POPs in polar bears; (ii) POPs may have negative impacts on survival and reproduction in polar bears, but these have not been demonstrated in the field; (iii) the impacts of POPs on polar bears may increase beyond effects caused by climate warming alone, and may interact with climate warming in causing negative effects on survival or reproduction.

1) Polar bears are subjected to two anthropogenic threats, loss of their habitat due to climate warming and exposure of pollutants, and 2) There are clear potentials that the two threats interact and thus have a larger effect on polar bears than the two threats alone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interacting consequences of climate change and pollutant exposure for polar bears.
how climate change, pollution and their interactions affect the population dynamics of a key Arctic species.
the interacting effects of climate warming and POP exposure on polar bears.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combined effect of climate warming and exposure of polar bears to POPs is likely to be more severe than the effect of climate warming alone, but this needs to be further investigated.

climate induced loss of polar bear habitat will have a negative effect on the population dynamics of polar bears, and that the negative effects of pollutant exposure will be enhanced by climate change.

climate change and POP exposure interact to cause population declines of polar bears, and that these effects are likely to be additive and not synergistic, i.e. the combined effect of the two stressors will be equal to or greater than the sum of the two stressor effects alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to consider both climate warming and pollutants in relation to polar bear health and survival, as well as in relation to the population level.
climate change and pollution are interacting threats to the health and survival of polar bears.
climate warming and pollutants are interacting threats to polar bears.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we need to consider the interacting consequences of climate change and POP exposure for polar bears, in order to fully understand the consequences of these anthropogenic stressors for polar bears, and in turn for the Arctic ecosystem.
there is a need for studies that address the interacting effects of climate change and pollutant exposure on wildlife populations.
the impacts of climate warming on polar bear populations are not limited to the direct impacts of loss of sea ice habitat.
